title: If and then
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: si takes the PRESENT and never the future: si tienes tiempo, si puedo, si llueve. English says "if it will rain" without blinking; Spanish has no such sentence at all. What follows the comma is free — present or future, both ordinary — so the rule is about one side of the sentence only.

si (if) and L1-M2's sí (yes) are two different words one keystroke apart. The accent is a letter, not decoration: si vienes is a condition and sí, vienes is an agreement. Nothing else in the sentence tells them apart, and a reader does not repair the wrong one.

The -ré future is built on the whole infinitive, endings added to the end of it: hablar → hablaré, ir → iré. Five verbs shorten the stem first and have to be learnt: haré (hacer), tendré (tener), podré (poder), diré (decir), vendré (venir). L1-M6's voy a + infinitive is not replaced by any of this — voy a is the near, spoken future and -ré is the more distant and more written one.

The conditional is the same stem as the future with -ía on it: iré → iría, podré → podría, tendré → tendría, haré → haría. Whatever shortening the future did, the conditional does too — which is why the two are learnt in one breath and never separately.

One counterfactual frame, and one only: si + tuviera / fuera, then the conditional — si tuviera tiempo, iría. It says a wish about something that is not so. tuviera and fuera are the imperfect subjunctive, and the rest of that mood — every other verb, every other cell — is a later level's.

sentences.display: Si tienes tiempo, te llamo mañana.
sentences.cue: If you have time, I'll call you tomorrow.
sentences.literal: If you-have time, to-you I-call tomorrow.

words.note: No accent, and that is the whole difference from L1-M2's sí, "yes". After it the verb is present, never future: si tienes tiempo, never si tendrás tiempo.

sentences.trap: English hears a future in both halves of "if you'll have time, I'll call". Spanish allows one at most, and never in the si half.
sentences.sound: si is one flat syllable, said exactly as English "see". No stress lands on it — the weight of the sentence is on tiempo.

variations.display: Si puedo, te llamo esta noche.
variations.cue: If I can, I'll call you tonight.
variations.changed: the condition made about the speaker

variations.cue: If you have time, we'll talk tomorrow.
variations.changed: the present standing in for a future on both sides

mistake.display: Si tendrás tiempo, te llamo mañana.
mistake.why: There is no future after si in Spanish: si tienes tiempo. English's "if you'll have time" is what builds the sentence, and no Spanish speaker would finish it.

sentences.usage: How every loose plan is made. The present in the si half is doing future work and nobody hears it as present.

sentences.display: Si llueve, no voy al parque. Si puedo, iré.
sentences.cue: If it rains, I'm not going to the park. If I can, I'll go.
sentences.literal: If it-rains, not I-go to-the park. If I-can, I-will-go.

words.note: Weather verbs have no subject at all — there is nothing to put in front of llueve, and Spanish has no word doing English's job of "it" here.
ir plus the future ending, with nothing shortened: ir → iré. L1-M6's voy a ir is the near, spoken future and this is the more distant one.

sentences.trap: Both halves of a si sentence can take a different tense from each other. The first stays present because it is a condition; the second says whenever it likes.
sentences.sound: YUE-be, with the ll a y sound and the v a soft b. i-RE, two syllables with the stress on the end, which is what the accent marks.

variations.display: Si llueve, no voy al cine.
variations.cue: If it rains, I'm not going to the cinema.
variations.changed: where the rain stops you going

variations.cue: If I can, I'll go on Saturday.
variations.changed: the future given its day

mistake.display: Si lloverá, no voy al parque.
mistake.why: The condition takes the present: si llueve. lloverá is a real word and it cannot stand after si, which is the one shape English speakers reach for.

sentences.usage: Weekend arithmetic, said out loud. The second sentence swaps to -ré because the going is further off and less certain.
sentences.mnemonic: It rains with nobody doing it.

sentences.display: Mañana tendré una reunión con mi jefe.
sentences.cue: Tomorrow I'll have a meeting with my boss.
sentences.literal: Tomorrow I-will-have a meeting with my boss.

words.note: tener shortens before the future ending — tener → tendr- → tendré — so it cannot be built from the infinitive whole. L2-M2's tengo is untouched by this.

sentences.trap: L1-M6 taught voy a and this module teaches -ré, and neither replaces the other. Voy a tener una reunión is the same appointment said in the near future.
sentences.sound: ten-DRE, stressed on the end. The d is there because the stem shortened, and it is fully said.

variations.cue: Tomorrow I'll have time.
variations.changed: what there will be

variations.display: Voy a tener una reunión mañana.
variations.cue: I'm going to have a meeting tomorrow.
variations.changed: L1-M6's near future in place of -ré

mistake.why: tener is one of the five that shorten: tendré. Adding the ending to the whole infinitive is exactly what works for hablar and exactly what fails here.

sentences.usage: Diary talk. The -ré future is what gets written in a message, where voy a is what gets said across a desk.
sentences.mnemonic: tener loses its e and gains a d.

sentences.display: No podré ir el sábado, pero haré algo el domingo.
sentences.cue: I won't be able to go on Saturday, but I'll do something on Sunday.
sentences.literal: Not I-will-be-able to-go the Saturday, but I-will-do something the Sunday.

words.note: poder shortens to podr- before the ending: podré. English has no future of "can" and reaches for "will be able to"; Spanish just conjugates the verb.
hacer shortens all the way to har-: haré. L1-M6's hacer and L1-M5's hice are the same verb, and none of its shapes look like the others.

sentences.trap: English cannot say "I will can", so it borrows a whole phrase. Spanish has the cell, and podré is one word where English needs four.
sentences.sound: po-DRE and a-RE, both stressed on the end, and the h of haré is silent as every Spanish h is.

variations.cue: I won't be able to go tomorrow.
variations.changed: the day

variations.cue: I'll do something on Sunday.
variations.changed: the second half standing alone

mistake.why: poder shortens before the ending: podré. The five that shorten are the whole of the irregularity, and poder is one of them.

sentences.usage: Turning down one invitation and offering another, which is what most of the future tense is for.
sentences.mnemonic: Five verbs shorten; podré and haré are two of them.

sentences.display: Te diré algo mañana. Vendré el sábado por la tarde.
sentences.cue: I'll tell you something tomorrow. I'll come on Saturday afternoon.
sentences.literal: To-you I-will-say something tomorrow. I-will-come the Saturday by the afternoon.

words.note: decir shortens to dir- before the ending: diré. L2-M10's dije and dijo are the past of the same verb, and no two of its shapes agree.
venir shortens and grows a d, exactly as tener does: venir → vendr- → vendré. The pair is worth learning together because they break the same way.

sentences.trap: tendré and vendré rhyme because tener and venir shorten identically. Learning one of them is learning both, and that is the only bargain this tense offers.
sentences.sound: di-RE, and ben-DRE with the v a soft b made with both lips. Both stressed on the final syllable.

variations.cue: I'll tell you something on Sunday.
variations.changed: the day

variations.cue: I'll come tomorrow morning.
variations.changed: when the coming happens

mistake.why: decir shortens to dir-: te diré algo mañana. The whole infinitive plus an ending is what regular verbs do, and decir is not one.

sentences.usage: Both halves of a promise. Spanish reaches for -ré here because the promise is for another day.
sentences.mnemonic: tendré and vendré break the same way.

sentences.display: Yo que tú, iría al médico hoy.
sentences.cue: If I were you, I'd go to the doctor today.
sentences.literal: I that you, I-would-go to-the doctor today.

words.note: A whole frame with no verb in it at all, where English needs four words and a subjunctive. It is fixed: nothing inside it changes, and it is tú-only.
The conditional of ir: the future stem iré plus -ía. Whatever the future did to a verb, the conditional does the same, which makes the pair one lesson.

sentences.trap: The frame has no verb, so there is nothing in it to conjugate. A learner building si yo fuera tú word by word has said something correct and heavier than anyone speaks.
sentences.sound: yo ke TU, three quick syllables with the stress at the end. i-RI-a is three syllables, the accent breaking the i away from the a.

variations.cue: If I were you, I'd go tomorrow.
variations.changed: when the advice says to go

variations.display: Yo que tú, no iría hoy.
variations.cue: If I were you, I wouldn't go today.
variations.changed: the advice reversed

mistake.display: Yo que tú, voy al médico hoy.
mistake.why: The frame is advice about a situation that is not yours, so the verb after it is conditional: yo que tú, iría. voy makes it a plan of your own.

sentences.usage: The everyday way to give advice without giving an order. Said between friends; the frame itself names tú, so it never reaches a stranger.
sentences.mnemonic: yo que tú carries no verb of its own.

sentences.display: ¿Podría ayudarme, por favor? Sería muy amable.
sentences.cue: Could you help me, please? That would be very kind.
sentences.literal: Could to-help-me, please? Would-be very kind.

words.note: The conditional of poder, and the politest way to ask for anything: ¿podría ayudarme? L2-M1's ¿puede? asks the same thing with less distance in it.
The conditional of ser, off the future stem seré: sería. One cell covers yo and él/ella, exactly as sea does.

sentences.trap: L2-M1 bought politeness with frames because this tense was not available yet. Now it is, and ¿podría? is a step above ¿puede? rather than a replacement for it.
sentences.sound: po-DRI-a, three syllables, and the question rises at the end even with the two question marks around it.

variations.cue: Could you repeat that, please?
variations.changed: what is being asked for

variations.cue: Could you open the window?
variations.changed: L2-M1's request rebuilt with the conditional

mistake.why: podría takes the infinitive with nothing between: ¿podría ayudarme? The a belongs to voy a, and it is the habit that puts it here.

sentences.usage: For a stranger, a counter, an office. The chip is formal because podría is what distance sounds like in Spanish.
sentences.mnemonic: puede asks; podría asks from further away.

sentences.display: Si tuviera más tiempo, iría al cine contigo.
sentences.cue: If I had more time, I'd go to the cinema with you.
sentences.literal: If I-had more time, I-would-go to-the cinema with-you.

words.cue: if I had · if he had
words.note: The imperfect subjunctive of tener, and here it says the opposite of what is true: si tuviera tiempo means the speaker has none. One cell for yo and él/ella.

sentences.trap: This si is not S01's. A present after si is a real condition; tuviera after si is a wish about something that is not so, and the second half moves to the conditional to match.
sentences.sound: tu-BIE-ra, with the v a soft b and the ie said as one glide. Three syllables, stressed in the middle.

variations.cue: If I had time, I'd go today.
variations.changed: the wish brought forward to today

variations.display: Si tengo tiempo, voy al cine.
variations.cue: If I have time, I'll go to the cinema.
variations.changed: the real condition beside the unreal one

mistake.display: Si tengo más tiempo, iría al cine.
mistake.why: A conditional in the second half needs tuviera in the first: si tuviera más tiempo, iría. tengo makes it a real condition, and then the going has to be voy.

sentences.usage: Turning something down while saying you wanted it. The frame is an apology as much as a condition.
sentences.mnemonic: tuviera says it is not so.

sentences.display: Si fuera más fácil, lo haría hoy. Tendría más tiempo.
sentences.cue: If it were easier, I'd do it today. I'd have more time.
sentences.literal: If it-were more easy, it I-would-do today. I-would-have more time.

words.cue: if it were · if I were
words.note: The imperfect subjunctive of ser, the second and last cell this module opens: si fuera más fácil. L1-M5's fue is the same verb in the past.

words.cue: I would do · I would make
words.note: The conditional of hacer, off the shortened future stem har-: haré, haría. The shortening happens once and both tenses use it.
The conditional of tener, off tendr-: tendré, tendría. Reading the two side by side is the cheapest way to see that the stem is shared.

sentences.trap: fuera and tuviera are the only two cells of this mood the module opens, and both live inside the same frame. Everything else the imperfect subjunctive does is a later level's.
sentences.sound: FUE-ra, two syllables with the ue as one glide, stressed at the front. a-RI-a and ten-DRI-a both break the i from the a.

variations.display: Si fuera más barato, lo haría.
variations.cue: If it were cheaper, I'd do it.
variations.changed: what would have to change first

variations.cue: I'd have more time on Sunday.
variations.changed: the conditional standing without its condition

mistake.display: Si sería más fácil, lo haría hoy.
mistake.why: The conditional never stands after si: si fuera más fácil. sería belongs on the other side of the comma, where the wish lands.

sentences.usage: Explaining why something is not happening. The second sentence shows the conditional living perfectly well on its own.

sentences.display: Si tengo tiempo, hablaré con mi jefe. Yo que tú, hablaría hoy.
sentences.cue: If I have time, I'll speak to my boss. If I were you, I'd speak today.
sentences.literal: If I-have time, I-will-speak with my boss. I that you, I-would-speak today.

words.note: L1-M6's hablaré with -ía in place of -é. hablar shortens nothing, so both tenses are the whole infinitive plus an ending, and the pair is visible in one line.

sentences.trap: hablaré came two levels ago and hablaría is one letter of work away from it. The module's whole conditional is that swap, applied to whatever stem the future already had.
sentences.sound: a-bla-RE against a-bla-RI-a: the second is a syllable longer and the stress moves onto the i.

variations.cue: If I have time, I'll speak tomorrow.
variations.changed: when the speaking happens

variations.display: Yo que tú, hablaría con tu jefe.
variations.cue: If I were you, I'd speak to your boss.
variations.changed: the advice given its listener

mistake.display: Si tendré tiempo, hablaré con mi jefe.
mistake.why: The si half is present, whatever the other half does: si tengo tiempo, hablaré. A future on both sides is the English sentence, word for word.

sentences.usage: A plan and the advice it earns, in one breath. Nothing here is new except the ending on the last verb.
sentences.mnemonic: -é is what will happen; -ía is what would.
